rv.q: Joe Mantello directs one hell of a show.
Mr. McPherson has crafted a genuinely scary piece of theater that makes effective use of the intimate Lyceum Theatre space to create an atmosphere of mounting dread.
It’s disturbing and gross in ways I personally haven’t seen on Broadway before.
There’s no show on Broadway quite like Grey House, a play that manages (at least until the end) to exhale hilarity and horror in the same icy breath.
I think it's a worthwhile challenge and one I'm not going to spoil.

The most haunted, haunting performance comes from Sophia Anne Caruso as Marlow...Cracking wise with aching vulnerability, Caruso is the insistent, irresistible heart of ‘Grey House’ and its sonorous death knell.
If it doesn’t fully succeed on its own terms, it’s at least a solid reminder that terror is as worthy of drama as any other kind of spectacle.
That teasing quality, though sometimes charming — and often, if you are a scaredy-cat, a relief from the hard-core jolts — is the giveaway that 'Grey House'
The production makes a good case for more full-on spookiness onstage, even if it’s a less convincing one for this play in particular.
“I’ve seen this movie,” Henry says.
Amid such excellent atmospherics, you may not care when the play itself creaks.

But apart from Laurie Metcalf’s enjoyable portrayal of an inscrutable mountain woman, and a set by Scott Pask out of the Grimms’ grimmest fairy tale, the play itself exists in a sort of gray zone — neither particularly terrifying nor profound.
But the problem is not that we’re reminded of Stephen King or Jordan Peele — it’s that the execution here is far worse, the second half is a slog and nobody knows what the hell is going on.
These raw-knuckled riddles are what drive Holloway’s challengingly experimental meditation on the predestination of pain.
Even so, the play, and Mr. Mantello’s witty, spooky production, will leave you with lingering, vexing questions to savor after the curtain falls.
Even with the likely post-performance discussions and musings about "meaning," the greatest strength of this production of Grey House is the consistency of its preternatural mood.
Grey House succeeds in subverting both the genre and audience expectations by weaving together a haunting story of horror and heart.
Grey House is frustratingly ambiguous but amusing and entertainingly frightening—although we are all in on the joke.
Grey House is an absorbing and often brilliant work, but it never quite lives up to its own potential.
Similarly, Grey House as a whole sometimes seems to get trapped between the all-too-human horrors of the murderer, the rapist, the abuser, and the grand guignol horrors of the haunted house.
Although the 110-minute production oozes mystery and a ghostly vibe, it doesn’t deliver intense shivers.
The actors work admirably hard in its quirkily baffling folds, but the story sticks and stops and starts and eventually disappears into itself.

Spectators who get Holloway’s full intentions, who follow his incriminating sentiments about the nectar of dead men origins will not only declare themselves scarily entertained but will continue considering the charges he has incorporated about man’s cruelty throughout the ages.
The new Broadway season has just begun, and it’s hard to imagine any future show proving more divisive.
But the show falls short for me, more an exercise in chills than a satisfying work of theater.
His direction exhausts every cliché of stage terror about half an hour into this 100-minute one-act.

Why a Tony-winning director like Joe Mantello and one of our most intelligent and perceptive actresses Laurie Metcalf (who does her best with the enigmatic Raleigh) would be involved in such a turkey is a bigger mystery than the one on stage.
This is the overly familiar premise of Levi Holloway’s bizarre, limp spook show Grey House now at the Lyceum, though probably not for very long.
The compelling new play doesn't frighten as much as it haunts and infuses, demanding curious attention.

For queer theatergoers looking for an occasional thrill without the typical Bury Your Gays trope, Grey House is entertaining enough, but for the price of a Broadway ticket, an overnighter at a haunted hotel might do the trick.
If you’re here for either horror or a captivating story from Broadway’s movie-length Grey House, prepare to walk away tragically disappointed.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this Broadway horror thriller, praising Metcalf's performance and atmospheric staging but faulting overly familiar tropes and tonal inconsistencies. Some find it genuinely scary; others call it derivative and unsatisfying.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.

vr.q: it was still definitely enjoyable and not the kind of theater experience you get to have on Broadway very often
